Good point about the other side of the tide. With regard to the spherical hollow earth thought experiment, the idea is that every point within the sphere experiences cancelling forces. Imagine a circle, for simplicity's sake. At the very center is a point equidistant to all points on the circumference by definition). So, naturally all forces acting on this point in the center will be in equal magnitude, but each force vector will have an opposing force vector canceling it out.

It gets interesting when you move away from center, but remain inside the circle. Suppose you move (1/2) * r in the +x direction (let r = radius). Symmetry still exists along the x-axis, and thus all y components of force vectors will have equal and opposing counterparts to cancel them out, thus there will be no net y component to the net force vector. But what about x? Being closer to the right side of the circle means that the gravitational force exerted by the mass along that part of the circle will be stronger than that on the left side of the circle. It might seem at first that this would cause an overall force in the +x direction. However, another thing to note is that a larger proportion of the circle's mass now resides to the left (-x) direction. Even though the force exerted by the left side of the circle is weaker per unit of mass along the circumference, there is a greater amount of mass to the left now. It turns out, after integrating the force vectors over all units of mass on the circumference, even the x component of the net force is cancelled out completely. This is true generally, for all points within the circle, and holds true in 3 dimensions as well, for a point within a sphere.

Regarding a person or object being torn apart, this is not a concern, because each unit of mass within the person / object experiences net force of zero, and thus no tugging or squishing will occur. Rather, it will be such that the object floats in a manner consistent with the complete absence of the surrounding sphere (as though it did not exist).
